name: If You Go Any Deeper You Might Come Out the Other Side
author: Shelf Community Press — Children's Safety Series, Vol. 7
description:
This story is read to children in the Shelf before they are old enough to go outside alone. Every child in Tier 1 knows it by heart. The illustrations — which cannot be reproduced here — are done in a style that is deliberately simple, almost cheerful, which makes the content worse.

Once there was a girl named Small Mara who lived on the fourth floor of a building that went down as far as it went up. Mara knew all the floors above her — the laundry on six, the clinic on eight, the roof where the pigeons glowed blue at night. But Mara did not know the floors below. Her mother said: don't go below the lobby. Mara said: why? Her mother said: because if you go any deeper, you might come out the other side. Mara did not understand this. She decided to find out.

Mara went to the lobby. The lobby had a door to the basement. The basement had stairs that went down. Mara went down. The first basement was full of pipes. The pipes were warm. The second basement was full of quiet. Not the quiet of an empty room — the quiet of a room that is listening. The third basement was smaller than the second, which was wrong because basements don't get smaller as you go down. The fourth basement was not there. Where the fourth basement should have been, there was a hallway. The hallway was long. The hallway was longer than the building was wide. Mara walked down the hallway. She did not look back because her mother had told her — though not about this hallway specifically — that passages shift when you look away.

At the end of the hallway was a room. The room had a chair. The chair had a person in it. The person looked like Small Mara but was not small. The person was old. The person opened her eyes and said: oh, you came. I have been waiting a very long time. You should not have come here. But since you did, let me tell you what I know: the tunnels do not go down. They go elsewhere. The deeper you go, the more elsewhere you get. And if you go deep enough, you come out the other side. The other side of what? said Mara. The old woman smiled and said: that's the wrong question. The right question is: which side are you on now?

Mara went back up the hallway. The hallway was shorter than before. The basements were in the wrong order — the quiet one was first, the pipes were last. The lobby was the same. Her mother was waiting. How long was I gone? said Mara. Her mother said: you weren't gone. Mara looked at the clock. No time had passed. But her shoes were dirty and she was very, very tired. She did not go below the lobby again.

The book ends with a page that has no illustration. It reads: "Your mother is right. Don't go below the lobby. The tunnels shift when you look away. The deeper you go, the more elsewhere you get. And the person in the chair at the end of the hallway is always you, but older, and always waiting, and always says the same thing: you should not have come here."

A handwritten note found inside a Shelf library copy of this book, in a child's handwriting: "I went. The chair was empty. That was worse."

story_hooks: A Shelf teacher notices that children who have read this book avoid specific stairwells — not all stairwells, specific ones. When asked why, they say the stairs go down too far. The teacher checks. The stairs go to the basement. Two floors. Normal. But the children insist: those stairs go further when nobody is looking.

A new edition of the book is being printed by the Shelf Community Press. The author — listed only as "M." — has added a final page to the new edition. The page contains a map. The map shows tunnels under the Shelf that do not appear on any official survey. The publisher says M. has not been contacted in person for six years. The manuscripts arrive by mail with no return address.
